questions.q: What is the main reason teams merge through pull requests instead of pushing to main?
questions.explain: A PR is a checkpoint: review catches what the author missed, and CI proves the combination with main still works. Branch protection makes the checkpoint mandatory.
options: Every change is seen by another person and passes automated checks before it can affect everyone
Git cannot merge branches without GitHub
Pull requests remove the need for tests

questions.q: Which bug report lets a developer start fixing immediately?
questions.explain: What happens, what should happen, how to reproduce it, and where: with those four parts nobody has to come back with questions.
options: "SAVE10 accepted but total stays ₦7,500; expected ₦6,750. Steps: add 3 socks at ₦2,500, enter SAVE10. Production, v1.0.0."

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "See #3" has no closing keyword, so it only links. "Closed #20" matches too, even though the author did not mean to close it: GitHub reads keywords, not intentions, so choose your words carefully in descriptions.

questions.q: Which commit subject follows the conventions from the lesson?
questions.explain: Imperative mood, a type, a specific description, short, no full stop. "Stuff" says nothing, and the last one is several commits' worth of changes in one.
options: fix: apply SAVE10 discount to cart total
update cart.js, README, tests and also the delivery fee logic which was wrong

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "Fix" is capitalised, so the type does not match. "docs:readme" is missing the space after the colon. chore!: is valid: the ! marks a breaking change.
questions.code:
const ok = (subject) => /^(feat|fix|docs|refactor|test|chore)(\([\w-]+\))?!?: [a-z]/.test(subject);
console.log(["feat(cart): add coupons", "Fix: rounding", "chore!: drop Node 20", "docs:readme"].map(ok));

questions.q: Which commit forces a new major version?
questions.explain: The ! (or a BREAKING CHANGE: line in the body) says existing users must change their code: every client reading amounts would now be off by a factor of 100.
options: feat(api)!: return amounts in kobo instead of naira
fix: round VAT to the nearest kobo

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The highest-ranking change wins: breaking beats feature beats fix. Tests and chores alone need no release at all.

questions.q: What is the key difference between merging main into your branch and rebasing your branch onto main?
questions.explain: After a rebase, bb6b965 became 586f4ea: same change, new commit. That is why a rebased branch must be force-pushed, and why shared branches should not be rebased.
options: Merge adds a merge commit and keeps existing commits; rebase replays your commits as new commits with new hashes
Merge loses your commits; rebase keeps them
There is no difference in the resulting history

questions.q: Which branch should you not rebase?
questions.explain: Never rebase commits others have based work on. Their copies still contain the old commits, and the next pull duplicates or loses work.
options: A release/2.0 branch that four teammates commit to and pull from
Your own feature branch that only you work on
A branch you have not pushed yet
A draft PR branch nobody else has checked out

questions.q: After git rebase origin/main, git push is rejected with "non-fast-forward", and the hint says to run git pull. What should you do?
questions.explain: git pull would merge the old, pre-rebase commits back in and give you two copies of every change. After a deliberate rebase you replace the branch, safely, with --force-with-lease.
options: git push --force-with-lease, because you intend to replace the remote branch with the rebased one
Delete the local branch and start again

questions.q: This simulates --force-with-lease. What does it print?
questions.explain: The lease is "the branch is still where I last saw it". A teammate's push (010d118) broke the lease, so the second force-push is refused instead of deleting their commit. Plain --force skips the check.
options:
forced update to 5f76cb9
rejected (stale info): server has 010d118

forced update to 5f76cb9
forced update to 9a1b2c3

rejected (stale info): server has f53e6e8
rejected (stale info): server has 010d118

forced update to 5f76cb9
rejected (stale info): server has 5f76cb9

questions.q: Your editor runs git fetch automatically in the background. Why can that weaken --force-with-lease?
questions.explain: The lease compares with your remote-tracking branch, which a background fetch moves. --force-if-includes adds a check that your branch actually contains what you fetched.
options: The fetch updates your "last seen" position to include a teammate's commit you never looked at, so the lease passes and the force-push deletes it
The lease only works with SSH
It cannot; the lease always compares with the teammate's machine

questions.q: During git rebase origin/main, a conflict appears. What does git checkout --ours cart.js keep?
questions.explain: A rebase replays your commits on top of main, so HEAD ("ours") is main and your commit is "theirs": the opposite of a merge. Read the marker labels rather than trusting the words.
options: The version from main (the base being rebased onto), not your commit
The original version before both changes

questions.q: What does the zdiff3 conflict style add to the markers?
questions.explain: With the original in view you can see what each side changed, and so what each person intended, which is what a correct resolution must keep.
options: A third section, after |||||||, showing the lines as they were before either side changed them
The names of the people who made each change

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both sides differ from the base: one changed the value, the other added a comment. A resolution should keep both: const fee = 150000; // naira, and whoever resolves it should notice that the comment is now wrong, since fees are in kobo.

questions.q: You resolved a conflict and the file has no markers left. What should you do before git rebase --continue?
questions.explain: Git only knows lines, not meaning. The lesson ran cartTotal after resolving and checked it returned 675,000 kobo before continuing.
options: Run the code or the tests, because a conflict-free file can still be a broken combination
Nothing, no markers means it works

questions.q: After a rebase you want your old commits back. They are on no branch any more. Where can you find them?
questions.explain: Git does not delete abandoned commits right away. The reflog lists them, and git reset --hard HEAD@{n} moves your branch back to one.
options: git reflog, which records every position HEAD had, for about 90 days

questions.q: Why is a 1,500-line pull request a problem even if the code is good?
questions.explain: Review quality drops quickly with size. Split big work into a series of smaller PRs that each make sense on their own.
options: Reviewers cannot review it carefully, so bugs slip through and it tends to get approved without real review
CI only tests the first 500 lines

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 12 + 3 + 40 + 0 + 2 + 2 = 59. The lockfile's 3,300 changed lines are generated, so a size check leaves them out.

questions.q: In CODEOWNERS, the last matching line wins. Who must review src/payments/refunds.js?
questions.explain: Later rules override earlier ones, so put general rules first and specific ones after. The payments README goes to the docs team because the *.md rule comes later; if payments must approve it too, add a more specific line at the end.

questions.q: Which GitHub setting prevents "someone pushed straight to main on Friday"?
questions.explain: Protection rules make the process mandatory instead of a habit. They can also block force-pushes and deletion of the branch.
options: A branch protection rule (or ruleset) on main requiring pull requests, approvals and passing checks

questions.q: A PR has 9 commits: 3 real steps and 6 "fix typo"/"wip". Which merge option gives main a clean history without asking the author to rewrite?
questions.explain: Squash turns the whole PR into one commit on main, titled after the PR. Rebase and merge would copy all nine commits, noise included.
options: Close the PR and ask for a new one

questions.q: After squash-merging a branch locally, git branch -d fix/save10-discount refuses and says the branch is not fully merged. Why?
questions.explain: The content is on main, but not those commits. After verifying, -D deletes the branch anyway.
options: The squash created a new commit; the branch's own commits are not ancestors of main, so Git cannot tell they were merged
The branch is still checked out on the server
Git never deletes branches with more than one commit

questions.q: What should a reviewer look at first?
questions.explain: Correctness, tests and security matter most. Formatting is the formatter's job, and naming comes after the code is right.
options: Whether the change does what the issue asks, correctly, including edge cases and tests
Whether the author used the reviewer's favourite style

questions.q: Which review comment is most useful?
questions.explain: It names the problem, gives a concrete case, suggests a fix, and says how important it is. It is about the code, not the person.
options: "question (blocking): what happens when the code is typed in lower case, like save10? Could we normalise it and add a test?"
"Why would you do it like this?"
"LGTM" on a 1,200-line change after two minutes

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The VAT bug is a real problem and blocks the merge. The nit and the suggestion are optional, and the praise tells the author what to keep doing.

questions.q: A reviewer asks for a change you disagree with. What is the professional response?
questions.explain: Disagreement with reasons is healthy; either you learn something or they do. Silence and workarounds destroy the trust review depends on.
options: Reply with your reasons; if it goes back and forth more than twice, talk directly and agree
Make the change silently, then undo it later

questions.q: Why should releases use annotated tags (git tag -a)?
questions.explain: A lightweight tag is only a name for a commit. An annotated tag is a real object that records who released what and when; npm version creates annotated tags.
options: They store a message, the tagger and a date, and tools such as git describe and --follow-tags use them
Annotated tags move with the branch

questions.q: This rebuilds git describe's answer from the history. What does it print?
questions.explain: Walking back from the newest commit, the first tag found is v1.1.0, one commit back. When the current commit is itself tagged, git describe prints just the tag.

questions.q: You tagged and pushed v1.2.0, then found a bug in it. What should you do?
questions.explain: Others may already have built, deployed or installed from v1.2.0. If the same name suddenly means different code, nobody can trust any version number.
options: Fix it and release v1.2.1; leave v1.2.0 where it is
Delete v1.2.0 and create it again on the fixed commit
Force-push the tag to the new commit

questions.q: Who is a changelog written for?
questions.explain: That is why refactors and test changes are usually left out, and why generated entries should be edited into plain language.
options: The people who use the software, who want to know what changed for them in each version
Only the developers who wrote the code
Git, which reads it to create tags

questions.q: In a fork workflow, what are origin and upstream?
questions.explain: You push branches to your fork and open the pull request from there into upstream. New work starts from upstream/main, which may be ahead of your fork.
options: origin is your fork, which you can push to; upstream is the original project, which you read from
origin is the original project; upstream is your fork
Both point to the same repository
upstream is the branch you are working on

questions.q: You want to add a large new feature to an open-source library you use. What should you do first?
questions.explain: Maintainers must support every line for years. Agreeing on the approach first saves you from a large PR being closed.
options: Read CONTRIBUTING.md and open an issue describing the plan, before writing the code
Write the whole feature and open a big PR
Fork it and publish your own version

questions.q: A commit's id is a hash of its content and its parent. This toy hash shows what a rebase does to ids. What does it print?
questions.explain: Same change, different parent, different id: that is why a rebased commit gets a new hash, and why the old commit still exists (in the reflog) until it is cleaned up. Recomputing with the same inputs always gives the same id.

questions.q: Branches move when you commit; tags do not. What does this print?
questions.explain: A branch is a pointer that follows your new commits. A tag stays on the commit it was given, which is exactly what makes "the code of v1.1.0" a stable answer.

questions.q: Write checkSubject(subject) that returns a list of problems: "format" if it is not type: description or type(scope): description (optionally with ! before the colon), "length" if it is longer than 72 characters, and "period" if it ends with a full stop.
questions.explain: Returning every problem (not just the first) gives the author one clear list to fix. Hooked into git commit or CI, a check like this keeps history machine-readable for the version and changelog tools.

questions.q: Write closedIssues(text) that returns the numbers of the issues a PR description closes: the words close, closes, closed, fix, fixes, fixed, resolve, resolves or resolved (any case), a space, then # and a number. Remove duplicates.
questions.explain: The i flag makes it case-insensitive, g finds every match, and a Set removes the duplicate #12 while keeping the first-seen order.

questions.q: Write nextVersion(current, subjects): a breaking commit (type!: or type(scope)!:) bumps major, any feat bumps minor, any fix bumps patch, and otherwise the version stays the same.
questions.explain: Check from the biggest bump down, so one breaking commit wins over any number of features. A minor bump resets the patch to 0, and a major bump resets both.

questions.q: Git finds the merge base (the last common ancestor) of two branches to know what each side changed. Write mergeBase(parents, a, b), where parents maps each commit to its parent (or null): collect all ancestors of a (including itself), then walk back from b until you meet one.
questions.explain: The branch and main split at 0522a2e, the "base" section in zdiff3 markers. In the second call, be838f2 is itself an ancestor of a7f6522, which is exactly the situation where a fast-forward is possible. Real history can have merge commits with two parents, which needs a slightly bigger search.

questions.q: A push is a fast-forward when the server's current tip is an ancestor of the commit you push. Write canFastForward(parents, serverTip, newTip) and use it to explain why a rebased branch needs a force-push.
questions.explain: The rebased commit 586f4ea sits on be838f2; the server's bb6b965 is not in its history. Accepting the push would drop bb6b965 from the branch, so Git refuses unless you force it.
questions.expected:
new commit on top: true
after a rebase:    false

questions.q: Write takeSide(text, side) that resolves every conflict in a file by keeping one side: "head" keeps the lines between <<<<<<< and =======, "incoming" keeps the lines between ======= and >>>>>>>. Lines outside conflicts are always kept. (This is what git checkout --ours/--theirs does, and why it is dangerous.)
questions.explain: Either choice silently throws away one person's work: the new fee or the unit comment. Picking a side is only right when you have checked that the other side's change is truly not needed.

questions.q: Write changelogSection(version, subjects) that returns the Markdown for one release: a ## version heading, then ### Added for feat commits and ### Fixed for fix commits (each as - description), leaving out other types and empty headings.
questions.explain: Everything after the first ": " is the description, whether or not there is a scope. The refactor is left out because users are not affected by it.
questions.expected:
## 1.1.0
### Added
- add delivery fee by state
### Fixed
- apply SAVE10 discount (#13)
## 1.1.1
### Fixed
- round to the nearest kobo
